title: Glider Performance Tool
text: Tools for choosing the right PAM glider for a study and planning its mission: what each platform can carry, how the platforms compare, how long a glider will last on a given mission, and where it can fly.

title: Glider Performance Tool
text:
How the project started
The project began at the NOAA Fisheries Glider Rodeo 2026 hackathon as a way to compare the PAM-equipped gliders that flew in the rodeo: how each platform was piloted, how well it navigated, how long its battery and storage lasted, and how much noise it made. While building that comparison it became clear that the same knowledge answers a bigger question that comes before any deployment: which glider, sensors and mission set-up suit this study? The tool has grown from a rodeo comparison into a general glider comparison and mission planning tool.

title: Glider Performance Tool
text:
The pages
From the rodeo

Glider Performance: what every glider actually did during the rodeo, split by mission mode. This is the only page built directly on rodeo data.

For choosing a glider and planning a mission

Glider Selection Dashboard: enter what the mission needs (depth, duration, sensors, PAM recorder) and see which gliders match.
Direct Comparison: Slocum and Seaglider factor by factor, from the pilots’ experience.
Study Design Tool: draw a study area, lay out transects, estimate survey distance and mission duration, check the bathymetry, and export waypoint files.
Endurance calculation for Slocum and Seaglider: how long a mission lasts with a given set of sensors and dive settings.

        Calculation assumptions
        
          Transects are generated at the selected compass orientation and clipped to the study polygon.
          For the lawnmower option, transect segments are alternated and connected in sequence; connector distance is included.
          Nominal travel rate is speed in knots × 1.852 km/nmi × 24 h/day.
          Dive-cycle horizontal distance is approximated as 2 × target depth / tan(glide angle), assuming a symmetric straight-line descent and ascent.
          Map dots represent estimated surfacing locations, not subsurface profile positions or commanded waypoints.
          With multiple gliders, route distance is divided evenly among vehicles for the duration estimate only; tracks are not yet spatially assigned to individual gliders.
        
      
    
  

  
    Depth-averaged currents
    What a glider would measure as its depth-averaged current (DAC) over the study area,
    from 0 m to the target depth (or the seabed, if shallower), for the months of the deployment. Taken from
    the Copernicus GLORYS12 reanalysis monthly climatology (1993–2016 mean), then flown along the
    generated route to see what the currents do to the survey duration.

      Arrows on map

        90th percentile--of grid cells × months

Month
Mean (m/s)
90th pct (m/s)

        How the current estimate is made
        
          Eastward and northward velocity (uo, vo) on GLORYS12's 1/12° grid and 50 depth levels, monthly climatology over 1993–2016, read directly from Copernicus Marine's public ARCO store for the grid cells around the study area.
          DAC in each grid cell is the thickness-weighted mean velocity from the surface to the target depth; where the model seabed is shallower, it is averaged to the seabed instead.
          Area statistics use the grid cells inside the study polygon (all cells in its bounding box if the polygon is smaller than one cell), pooled across the deployment months.
          Along the route, the glider is assumed to crab into the current to hold its track: ground speed = along-track current + √(speed² − cross-track current²). Where the cross-track current is stronger than the glider, or the result is not forward progress, the track cannot be held; that distance is left out of the duration and reported instead.
          If more than 5 % of the track cannot be held, the duration is shown as not feasible rather than as a number.
          Duration with currents is the average over the deployment months of the duration flown in each month's currents; the worst month is shown beside it.
          Monthly climatological means smooth out tides, eddies, storms and inter-annual variability. Currents on a given day can be considerably stronger than these values — treat them as a typical background, not a bound.
        
      
    
    Currents: E.U. Copernicus Marine Service Information, Global Ocean Physics Reanalysis
    (GLOBAL_MULTIYEAR_PHY_001_030, monthly climatology), doi:10.48670/moi-00021.

title: Glider Performance
text:
Every glider in the rodeo flew the same plan: a shakedown, then fast,
slow, intermediate and drift blocks, then a short
repeat of slow, intermediate and fast at the end (the mini-modes, right of the hairline in each
panel). Because the modes are shared, the differences below are differences between the
platforms, not between missions. Numbers come from
output/glider_performance_summary.xlsx; each panel keeps its own y-axis, because a watt
and a cubic centimetre do not belong on one scale.



  
    Gliders
  
  
    Modes
  
  
    Metrics
  




Tradeoff explorer

The mission modes exist to answer what speed costs. Put one metric on each axis and every
glider-mode combination becomes a point, so the shape of the tradeoff shows up directly. Connect
the modes to follow one glider through the plan.


  
    X
    Y
     Connect modes
  
  
    Presets
  



Ranking

Every glider-mode combination on one metric, sorted. This is the view for “who used the least
energy per kilometre” — and for seeing how much of the spread is the platform and how much
is the mode it was flying.


  
    Metric
  



Mode comparison

The same numbers as a grid: one row per glider, one column per mode. Gaps are combinations with no
data rather than zeroes.


  
    Metric
  



Data recorded

How much raw data each system actually wrote during the rodeo. The deployments were not the same
length, so the per-day figure is the fairer comparison between PAM systems — and the spread is
mostly channel count and sample rate, not platform.


  
    Total recordedGB
    
    
  
  
    Recording rateGB/day
    
    Total raw data divided by the length of that glider’s deployment.
  


Efficiency

Two sections above ask what a kilometre cost and how much each system recorded. This divides
one by the other: how far a glider went, and how much it wrote, for every kilowatt‑hour it
spent. Up and to the right is more of both for the same energy. Neither axis is the
answer — a platform can buy data with distance, and the fastest way to look efficient on
the vertical axis is to record at a high bit rate.




The numbers

Every value on this page, for the gliders, modes and metrics selected above. Hover is a
convenience; this table is the source.



Platforms
One row per glider: what it is, how long it flew, what it recorded, and how its energy use was measured.

    Endurance is battery capacity by chemistry and bay
    (550 / 800 Ah primary, 215 / 300 Ah rechargeable) divided by total Ah per day, where the
    glider-and-standard-sensor load comes from the workbook's component power model and the
    external payload is added on top. Distance assumes 20 km/day.
    The external payload is read from content/data/extra-sensors.csv rather than
    from the workbook, so a sensor can be added, removed or re-costed by editing one line in the
    repository. The workbook hardcoded the same four inside a single formula; the replacement is
    checked against it on every build. Figures marked * carry a note
    — hover the name to read it.
    The workbook also reports a bare-glider endurance from the same power model. It is not
    shown here: it excludes the external sensors, so on these defaults it reads about five times
    longer and answers a different question.
